## Jeremiah 21: verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- The book isn't in date order. Chapter 21 jumps about 20 years past chapter 20, to Babylon's final siege of Jerusalem (Kidner dates it around 588 BC). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- This Pashhur is not the Pashhur son of Immer who put Jeremiah in the stocks (20:1–2). Several sources agree on this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/ ; https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21
- **Who this Pashhur was (commentators disagree):**
  - JFB says he was a priest of the fifth priestly order, and Zephaniah of the twenty-fourth. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say he is never called a priest. They think he was a royal official, since Jer 38:4 calls the same men "princes." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-1.htm
  - Constable also points to Jer 38:1–13 and denies he is the temple officer of chapter 20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html
- Zephaniah was the "second priest," assistant to the high priest (Jer 52:24; 2 Kgs 25:18). https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-1.htm
- **What the delegation shows:**
  - Barnes: by sending these men, Zedekiah treated Jeremiah the way Hezekiah treated Isaiah (2 Kgs 19:2). He adds that both envoys belonged to the party that wanted armed resistance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Coffman: the 597 BC exile had confirmed Jeremiah's preaching and made him a national figure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-21.html
- JFB also suggests the chapter belongs between chapters 37 and 38, because 38:2 quotes 21:9 and the same men appear in 37:3 and 38:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-1.htm
- **Zedekiah's character:**
  - Poole calls him "none of the best... none of the worst." His failing was that his corrupt court led him easily, more than stubbornness of his own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
  - JFB: he had some reverence for sacred things but no moral courage. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm

**v. 2**
- **Which "past wonders" Zedekiah meant:**
  - Most commentators say he was thinking of God lifting Sennacherib's siege in Hezekiah's day (2 Kgs 18–19). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm ; https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
  - Barnes says the king expected an answer like Isaiah's in Isa 37:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Constable adds Jehoshaphat's deliverance (2 Chr 20). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html
- **A request with no repentance:**
  - Meyer (quoted by Guzik): the people wanted to escape the consequences of their sins more than they wanted to repent. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - Matthew Henry: people often turn in distress to ministers they despised in good times, but only to escape punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/21.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary homilies (Muir, Young) say the king appealed to God's power rather than his grace. There is no confession, no repentance and no promise to change. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-21.html
  - Utley: Zedekiah wanted God's covenant mercy without covenant faithfulness. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21
- Barnes notes "Nebuchadrezzar" is the more accurate spelling. Constable says this is the first time Jeremiah mentions him, and that he ruled 605–562 BC. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html

**v. 3**
- **Jeremiah's boldness:**
  - Guzik praises Jeremiah for speaking so plainly to a king. Trapp says he answered modestly but boldly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - Poole: being honoured by a royal delegation didn't tempt the prophet to say pleasant things God hadn't given him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm

**v. 4**
- Their own weapons would be useless, and the Babylonians would break into the middle of the city. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- JFB: God would turn the weapons to a use very different from what they intended. He quotes Calvin, who says God stays "the God of Israel" even while destroying the faithless king, because it is Judah that has lost the covenant privileges. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
- Barnes: grammatically, "outside the walls" goes with "with which you fight." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm

**v. 5**
- Judah would be fighting God himself, not just Babylon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- Pulpit (Young): this is not just men against men. It is people who have forsaken God against the nation God is using to carry out his righteous anger. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-21.html
- Poole: "hand," "arm" and "fury" describe God in human terms. God has no body, and his anger is not a turbulent passion. The words mean his just will to punish. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
- "Outstretched hand… mighty arm" is Exodus language. Bible.org (Utley) and Guzik both say the "wonders" Zedekiah hoped for would now be turned against Judah. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/

**v. 6**
- Disease would kill as many people as the war. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- Coffman: people and animals crowded into the besieged city would overwhelm its sanitation and set off an epidemic. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-21.html
- Utley: when an enemy invaded, villagers crowded into the walled cities, and food, water and sanitation broke down. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21

**v. 7**
- **How it was fulfilled:**
  - Guzik: Zedekiah's sons were killed in front of him, then he was blinded and taken to Babylon (2 Kgs 25:7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - JFB: the sword fell on his sons and the nobles. Zedekiah himself died of grief rather than violently. JFB also reads "the people" as meaning "those who are left." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
  - Constable takes the verse to mean Nebuchadnezzar would kill the king as well. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html
- Feinberg: "put them to the sword" means killing without mercy. Trapp notes the Hebrew experts singled this out as a very long verse (42 words), which "sounds very heavily." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- "Sword, famine and plague" is the standard description of a siege. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21

**v. 8**
- **Echo of Deuteronomy:**
  - The words echo Deut 30:15, 19. Guzik adds Josh 24:15 and 1 Kgs 18:21. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - Coffman says the wording is taken almost word for word from Deut 30:15–20. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-21.html
- **What "life" means here (an important difference in emphasis):**
  - Several commentators stress that this is not Moses' offer of blessing. Matthew Henry calls it a "melancholy dilemma": choose the lesser of two evils, captivity rather than death. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-8.html
  - An unnamed commentator on Biblehub's page (written like Ellicott) says "life" here doesn't mean eternal blessedness. It simply means surrendering to Babylon and living in exile and poverty. Another unnamed note on the page says "life" means only escaping death, not prosperity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-8.htm
  - Utley: "life" here is physical deliverance, while the Deuteronomy passage is about the blessings of keeping the covenant. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21
  - The Geneva Study Bible notes: life = surrendering to Nebuchadnezzar; death = resisting him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-8.htm
- NET note: the Hebrew word order sets this message to the people apart from the message to Zedekiah (v. 3). https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Jer+21%3A8%2C9&mode=print

**v. 9**
- **Treason? (a point every source addresses):**
  - Poole: if anyone ever spoke "high treason," Jeremiah did here. His only excuse is that this was a revelation from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Barnes: this would be treason from an ordinary man, but prophets spoke with an authority above the king's. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Guzik: Jeremiah wasn't pro-Babylon. He was "pro-Yahweh." Thompson (quoted there): accepting God's judgment was the first step toward renewal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - Chuck Smith: this message got Jeremiah accused of treason and imprisoned. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-8.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary (Conway) quotes Stanley: his advice came from loyalty to the nation's lasting interests, not indifference. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-21.html
- **"His life like a spoil of war":**
  - NET note: spoil is what the victor carries off. Those who surrendered would lose property, freedom and citizenship but escape with their lives. Since God had decided to destroy the city, this was the wise course. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/b/o/passage.php?passage=Jer+21%3A8%2C9&mode=print
  - Barnes: like loot snatched in danger, they would carry their lives off as more than they had a right to. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Poole calls it a proverbial phrase. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
  - TGC: those who honour Nebuchadnezzar as the new rightful king will keep their lives "as prizes of war." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
- **Spiritual application:**
  - Meyer (via Guzik) links this to Jesus' saying that whoever loses his life will save it. Guzik's principle: when we fight God, our only hope is to surrender. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - The Pulpit homilies (Spanish translation on StudyLight) say this way of escape illustrates the Christian way of salvation: safety is found in submission. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/spa/tpc/jeremiah-21.html
  - Matthew Henry: no sinner is left without a refuge, but the way of life is humbling and demands self-denial. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/21.htm
  - Coffman sees Jeremiah here as a type of Christ, since both told the faithful to leave Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-21.html

**v. 10**
- Poole: "set My face against" means God has decided to bring ruin, not just withdrawn his favour. "Burn it with fire" refers mainly to the city's buildings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): fulfilled literally in Jer 52:13. Burning a captured city was common but not universal. Ellicott thinks the reply to the delegation may have ended here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-10.html
- Constable: the decision was fixed, and neither actions nor prayers could change it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html

**v. 11**
- **Where vv. 11–14 belong (a real interpretive debate):**
  - Barnes: drop the word "say." This verse opens a longer section (to 23:8) that gathers earlier messages to the royal house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
  - NET note: some read vv. 11–14 as part of the reply to Zedekiah. NET thinks it is more likely a heading, "Now concerning the royal court," parallel to "concerning the prophets" at 23:9. It gives three reasons, including that a call to repent here would soften the judgment already announced. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php/verse.php?book=Jer&chapter=21&verse=11
  - Guzik/Feinberg: because the section still holds out hope, it may come from before the siege. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - TGC: 21:11–23:8 applies the surrender principle to the kings. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/
- Poole: "house of the king" means Zedekiah's court and officials. Even the great are bound to obey God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm

**v. 12**
- **"Every morning":**
  - Is it the time courts sat, or a way of saying "promptly"? Clarke (via Guzik) and Poole allow either. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
  - JFB: mainly proverbial, meaning "promptly." Maurer translates it "every morning." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-12.htm
  - Gill: get to it early and settle cases quickly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-12.html
  - Calvin: good judges decided cases in the morning, while in corrupt times rulers spent the morning drinking. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-12.html
  - Matthew Henry: don't sleep off last night's excess (cf. Eccl 10:16). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-12.html
  - Utley: probably at the city gate, early each day. https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-21
- **The king's duty:**
  - Barnes: the king judged cases in person, and the "oppressor" was usually a powerful noble, so it fell to the king to protect the weak. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/21-12.html
  - Guzik connects this to Rom 13:1–7, God's purpose for civil government. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- **Could repentance still avert judgment? (Protestant commentators differ):**
  - Guzik/Harrison: Jeremiah still hoped, though in vain, that quick reform would avert disaster. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
  - JFB: the decree was already issued. Righteousness could only lessen the punishment, not escape it entirely. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
- "House of David" rebukes them for falling so far from David's godliness, and for assuming their descent made them safe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/21-12.htm
- TGC: the kings in fact increased the oppression of the weak. The image of fire consuming a forest recurs (21:12, 14; 22:7). https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/jeremiah/

**v. 13**
- Jerusalem is addressed. Harrison: it had valleys on three sides. Feinberg: the Hebrew uses the feminine, so the city is meant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/
- JFB: Robinson identifies the "rocky plateau" as Mount Zion, where the royal palace stood. That fits a message to the house of David. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
- Poole: no natural position or fortification can stand against Almighty God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/jeremiah/21.htm
- Matthew Henry: "If God be for us, who can be against us? But if he be against us, who can do anything for us?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/jeremiah/21.htm

**v. 14**
- **What the "forest" is:**
  - It may be the palace called the "House of the Forest of Lebanon" (1 Kgs 7:2). Thompson suggests this (via Guzik), and Constable agrees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-21/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jeremiah-21.html
  - JFB: it means the dense mass of cedar houses. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm
  - Coffman sides with Keil that the city itself was "a forest of houses." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jeremiah-21.html
  - Barnes: to a Jewish hearer, "forest" suggested everything grand and stately. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/jeremiah/21.htm
- JFB points to Prov 1:31 and Isa 3:10–11 for "fruit of your doings." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jer/Jer_021.cfm

---

### Where the traditions really differ
I found no clear split by denomination in this chapter. The differences I did find are between individual commentators:
- Whether vv. 11–14 still offer real escape (Guzik, Harrison) or only a lighter punishment (JFB).
- Whether vv. 11–14 continue the reply to Zedekiah or begin a new section (NET, Barnes).
- How far to apply "the way of life" spiritually. Guzik, Meyer, the Pulpit homilies and Matthew Henry apply it to the gospel. The unnamed Biblehub commentators and Utley limit it to physical survival.

I didn't find any denominational teachers from the Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal or Lutheran sites. Ellicott is labelled Anglican on StudyLight, and Calvin is quoted on v. 4 (in JFB) and v. 12. Running more searches would be the next step for the missing groups.
